name: Vapor rub ointment (chest rub applied to the skin)
short: Case reports, mostly misuse (nose, eyes, swallowed, heated): organ failure, seizures, pneumonia, eye burns, toddler breathing distress. Skin: irritation, allergy; other camphor balms poisoned infants.
text: These data are for vapor rub ointment applied to the skin of the chest and neck. The page's trial abstract does not name its product or list its ingredients; most of the case reports below concern one widely sold vapor rub, which a 2010 case report describes as containing turpentine, eucalyptus and cedar leaf oils, camphor, menthol, nutmeg oil and thymol, so they are not necessarily about the trial ointment. In the trial, 138 children aged 2 to 11 with night-time cough and colds had vapor rub, petrolatum or no treatment applied to the chest and neck for one night, and irritant adverse effects were more common with vapor rub; the authors describe them as mild. Serious harms in case reports mostly followed use other than on chest skin. A 2025 narrative review of 37 articles on the widely sold product collected case reports of lipid pneumonia (11), eye injury (5), camphor toxicity (5), skin conditions (3), psychosis (1) and respiratory distress (1), and says many of the complications described, such as multi-organ failure, surgical removal of the eye's contents (ocular evisceration) and severe pneumonia, involved misuse; the review aims to guide patients, for example to avoid heating or swallowing the product or applying it in the nose, mouth or eyes. Swallowing by children: of 251 children reported to a Toronto poison information centre from December 1995 to March 1997 as having swallowed an essential oil or an essential-oil product, 90 involved the widely sold vapor rub; the most common symptoms were cough and vomiting, and two children had seizures but recovered; the authors' literature search found 18 reports of children swallowing such oils or products, with vomiting, lethargy, coma and seizures, and one child died; the abstract does not say which products caused the seizures or the death. Individual case reports describe: exogenous lipid pneumonia in an 85-year-old woman who had applied it continuously to her nostrils for chronic rhinitis (two years after she was advised to stop, the lung shadow had shrunk by about 10%); exogenous lipoid pneumonia in a 66-year-old man who applied a commercial vapor rub to his nostrils daily and also deliberately inhaled nebulised fluids containing scented oils; a paranoid psychosis lasting several months and an acute delirium in a woman who had abused a decongestant nasal spray together with the vapor rub, which reversed when she stopped both (so the case cannot separate the two products); severe respiratory distress in a toddler after it was applied directly under her nose (described by the authors of a ferret laboratory study as a patient they cared for; a title-only letter from the same year describes a vapor-rub study as an incomplete case report with misleading publicity, without the title saying which report it answers); a severe combined chemical and thermal eye burn in a 77-year-old woman from product heated in a microwave oven, needing an amniotic membrane transplant, cataract surgery and a corneal transplant; and an intoxication presenting as iron deficiency anaemia with minimal liver impairment (the abstract does not give the route). Title-only records report intoxication presenting as multi-organ failure, a late seizure after it was swallowed, lipoid pneumonitis after it was inhaled, inflammation of the skin, cornea and conjunctiva around the eye, and one-sided narrowing of the pupil after eye exposure to vapor rub ointment. On the skin, case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis after it was applied, lichen planus pigmentosus-like dark pigmentation of the face, and chemical leukoderma (loss of skin colour) linked to the thymol in an over-the-counter decongestant product. Labelled note on camphor from a different product (not vapor rub): a 1987 case report describes camphor and balsamic oil poisoning in a 1-month-old infant after a camphorated balsam ointment was applied to the skin, and its authors say that camphor and volatile oils are toxic to the central nervous system and of no therapeutic use in children. Further labelled notes on other products with the same kinds of ingredients (not vapor rub): a 1976 report attributes acute poisoning in an infant to skin absorption of camphor, menthol and thymol from a counterirritant salve, and its authors call for particular attention to poisoning from skin application of active substances in newborns and infants; case reports describe a brief, self-limited tonic-clonic seizure in a healthy 4-year-old girl after an over-the-counter eucalyptus oil head lice preparation was applied to her skin as directed, with rapid recovery after the skin was washed, and slurred speech, unsteadiness and muscle weakness progressing to unconsciousness in a 6-year-old girl after widespread skin application of a home remedy containing eucalyptus oil, with her symptoms resolved six hours after it was removed and no long-term after-effects; and a small case series describes status epilepticus in a young adult with post-traumatic epilepsy after various balms containing eucalyptus and camphor were applied to the skin. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
